1:
Three voices begin by correcting the heading. John Gill notes that some render it concerning Moab rather than against Moab, since the chapter closes in its favour; Charles Ellicott prefers the same, taking the words as the title of the section; and John Calvin reports that all the versions but one read to Moab and join the words to what follows, though the best rendering is concerning. Gill adds a dating from Josephus, about five years after the destruction of Jerusalem. Calvin explains why this nation is a special case. The Moabites came of Lot and were of one blood with the Israelites, who passed through their borders doing them no harm because God spared them for Lot’s sake; they were therefore not aliens like the Egyptians but intestine enemies. Ellicott sets out the later history, in which Moab was tributary under Ahab, revolted under Mesha, and was beaten by Israel, Judah and Edom together; he notes too that Jeremiah follows the older burden of Moab in even fuller detail.

The detail is what Ellicott works on. Nebo he identifies with the summit of Pisgah from which Moses looked upon the land of promise. Kiriathaim he reads as the double city, never identified. Misgab he calls the high fort or citadel, referred by some to Kir-Moab; and because the Hebrew prefixes the article, a lexicographer he cites takes it for the highland country of Moab generally. Calvin doubts it is a name at all, since two of the versions decline to treat it as one and no such place is found elsewhere; the rendering he reports is simply the high fortress.

At the second verse the voices delight in the wordplay. Adam Clarke marks a double paronomasia, a figure in which the prophets delight, Heshbon echoing the verb for devising and Madmen the verb for being struck dumb. Ellicott finds the same assonance, notes that a cognate form is elsewhere translated dunghill, and thinks the ignominious meaning may be why each prophet chose the name; three old versions render the clause in silence thou shalt be made silent, which he judges probably wrong. Calvin accepts it and supposes the versions read a different word, adding that to be silenced in prophetic language is to be subdued, in contrast with the boasting at the head of the verse. He and John Wesley agree on the history of the city: taken from Moab, held by Israel, recovered when Moab grew strong, and now lost again, the enemy sitting in council there. Matthew Henry makes the shame general: they shall be ashamed of the mighty boasts they once made of these cities.

Then the flight. Gill reports from Kimchi and Ben Melech that there were two Horons, an upper and a lower, the name being dual; Calvin says he does not know why they make one part higher than the other, since the place lay in a level country with mountains around it. Keil and Delitzsch add that one scholar takes Moab here for the old capital in the Arnon valley rather than the country. Over the little ones the division is sharpest. Ellicott holds that the word is the same as the name of the little city Zoar, so that the little ones are cities and not children. Calvin knows that reading and rejects it: children are far more emphatic, since men and women howl at a threatening while little children are moved by nothing but present evils, so that their crying proves the calamity extreme. Henry allows either the meaner sort of people or the children, whose cries are the most piteous. On the ascent Calvin observes that weeping is named twice to show that they wept the whole way up; and he notes that fear and shame both restrain tears, since an enemy will deride our weeping, so that to weep with the enemy in sight measures the grief.
6:
Whether the call to flee is meant kindly is the first question. John Gill allows that it may be the Moabites crying to one another, or the prophet counselling flight, as Abarbinel held; but others take it ironically, and that he calls the truest sense. Charles Ellicott hears the same irony at the ninth verse, where no prayer is left but to wish for the wings of a bird, and John Calvin calls that verse a bitter derision, meant not to goad the Moabites but to pierce them through. The comparison in the sixth verse divides them further. Adam Clarke reads the word as the name Aroer, which some take for a city and others for a blasted or withered tree, and locates a place of that name northward among the Ammonites. Ellicott takes the stunted shrub of the desert as the type of desolation and finds a play on the city’s name, remarking that one old version strangely gives a wild ass instead. Calvin reports renderings of tower and of a shepherd’s cot, prefers tamarisk or juniper, a barren tree that never grows because no rain cherishes it, and still thinks a city is meant. Keil and Delitzsch deny that it can be a town here at all.

What Moab trusted in divides them five ways. Gill offers the fortifications about their cities, which he says is the sense of two old versions, then the cattle preferred by Kimchi and Ben Melech, then their idols, which fits the threat against their god that follows. John Wesley gives it flatly as their idols. Calvin admits the herds as a possible exposition but leans to fortifications, since treasures are named beside it. Ellicott objects that the word is not used of fortresses elsewhere and thinks Moab is rather relying on its past achievements and deeds of prowess. Keil and Delitzsch survey the field, reject an emendation, reject the reference to idols on the ground that idols are always called works of hands, reject the rendering property as unsupported, and abide by the common meaning of works, not evil deeds specially but everything Moab undertakes.

On the god who goes into captivity with his priests the voices supplement each other. Clarke notes that ancient idolaters took their gods with them to the field of battle, and supposes it done in imitation of the Israelites and the ark. Ellicott notes that it was worshipped by the Ammonites too, that Solomon introduced and Josiah abolished its worship at Jerusalem, that Jerome identified it with Baal-peor, and that the Moabite Inscription makes it the deity who subdues the people of his rival. Calvin observes the double confidence the prophets always attack, earthly power set against God and reliance on idols, and says the princes who seemed to lie safe under that shadow go into exile with it.

The curse at the tenth verse produces the sharpest quarrel in the passage. Calvin says the words are addressed to the Chaldeans, urging them on as a general chides idling soldiers, and that the passage has been very absurdly explained by those who quote it to mean that we must omit nothing God commands; they misrepresent it, he says. Gill expounds it in precisely the way Calvin condemns, first of the Chaldeans commissioned not to spare, then as a general rule for all divine service, done deceitfully when men play the hypocrite and negligently when they are lukewarm. Keil and Delitzsch settle the adverb as carelessly rather than deceitfully. Clarke rests the severity on the sovereign right of the Author of life over lives long since forfeited. Ellicott, who calls the destruction a righteous retribution the prophet could not wish done by halves, adds a qualification none of the others makes: nations fighting slave-traders or pirates might legitimately echo the prayer, but it has been used with far less justification in the religious wars of his own country.
11:
The figure of wine left on its lees is worked by every voice, and they disagree about the wine. Adam Clarke explains that vintners let wine rest on its lees because this improves its strength and flavour, and rack it off only when that work is done. John Calvin adds the reason: the dregs preserve the wine, and wine drawn off from them loses part of its strength and at length becomes vapid. Charles Ellicott reverses it: the pouring from vessel to vessel is what clarifies wine and improves its flavour, and wine not so treated keeps its first crude bitterness. Keil and Delitzsch divide the cases: good wine becomes stronger and more juicy by lying long on its lees, while inferior wine becomes harsh. The application is the same either way. John Wesley puts it in a line, that this is why they keep their old sins, their pride and presumption and luxury; and Ellicott draws the moral out, that it is not good for nations to remain too long in a prosperity which strengthens their natural arrogance, since there is a wholesome discipline in defeat and even in exile; he points to the last verse of the chapter as the hope that it will do its work.

On the history behind the figure they are agreed. Clarke observes that Moab had been very little molested by war since he was a nation and never went out of his own land, and that apart from a few carried away by Shalmaneser he had known neither war nor captivity. Calvin compares him to an old man who has passed his whole life without a loss, and dates the childhood of the nation from the time they expelled the giants and took their land. John Gill makes the ease itself the cause of the pride the nation was notorious for, then turns the verse into a portrait of the unregenerate, who are sinners from birth and under sentence, yet feel no burden of guilt and no fear of hell, from hardness of heart and thoughtlessness about their own souls.

Calvin alone asks what the verse was for. It was very hard, he says, for the faithful to watch God afflict them while the Moabites sat safe and lost nothing; so the prophet tells them not to envy that happiness, since God will stretch out his hand at last, and he sets the passage beside those psalms which bid the faithful wait for the day of the Lord rather than fret at the prosperity of the ungodly.

The wanderers of the next verse prove to be a technical term. Clarke reports a rendering of tilters, those who tip a cask up at one end when it is nearly run out so that the last of the liquor may be drawn off, and thinks it well supported by the emptying of the vessels that follows. Calvin runs through incliners and strewers and plunderers and overturners, and judges tilters the best of them. Wesley keeps the plain sense, that they are the Chaldeans who wandered out of their own country to conquer other people, and Ellicott notes that the vessels and bottles are the cities and villages of Moab; Gill adds a date from Josephus, five years after the fall of Jerusalem. At the last verse the comparison of Chemosh with Bethel is read the same way by all: Clarke and Wesley identify Bethel by the golden calves, Ellicott says the name of the sanctuary stands for the calf worshipped there as a symbol of the true God, and Keil and Delitzsch make Moab perish with its god as Israel was dishonoured through its own. Calvin presses it home, that the prophet is not really addressing Moab but his own people, holding up the ruined ten tribes before Jews who kept the temple and the outward form while filling the sanctuary itself with idols.
14:
The boast is answered at once. John Gill says the Moabites were proud, boasting of their bodily strength and their skill in war as much as of their fortified cities, and thinking themselves a match for any enemy. John Calvin puts the same charge in his own terms: when all things prosper, ungodly men are moved by no fear and grow so sunk in indifference that they disregard not only the true God but everything that binds a conscience. Against that he sets the threatening, that God will reduce to nothing whatever they take for their protection. Matthew Henry notices what makes the blow terrible, that they were secure and thought themselves able to deal with the most powerful enemy, so that the calamity comes without time even to keep the enemy in parley; and he remarks that it takes more than ordinary courage not to be afraid of sudden fear.

Henry then declines the work the others are doing. In reading so long a roll of threatenings, he says, it is of more use to be possessed with a holy awe of God than to enquire critically into all the lively figures and metaphors here used. Calvin does enquire, and finds the fifteenth verse contested. The verb rendered gone up he takes transitively, so that the spoiler comes up against the cities; but it may be the inhabitants who go up and away, since the word can mean to vanish like smoke, and neither the versions nor the critics agree. He offers as the easiest construction that the waster of Moab and of its cities is gone up, and observes that going up belongs to the conqueror and going down to the conquered. Gill adds that the destruction is spoken of as past though future, after the manner of prophecy, because it is certain. Henry draws the sharper point: they went down to the battle promising themselves that they should return victorious, and God told them they were going down to the slaughter, so sure are those to fall against whom God fights.

That the calamity is near is what Calvin dwells on longest, and he says plainly whose comfort it is. It was a bitter trial for the faithful to be chastened while the wicked were spared, and delay tended to drive them toward despair; so the prophet tells them to strengthen their minds for a little while. He guards the promise against the passage of time by the rule that a thousand years are as one day with God, and by the charge in Habakkuk to wait for a prophecy that seems to delay. From this he draws a doctrine running both ways: whatever God promises we ought to receive as present though it is hidden and remote, and whatever he threatens ought to move us as though we saw his hand already armed with a sword. Gill and John Wesley both date it from Josephus, five years after Jerusalem fell.

The call to bemoan divides them. Gill takes it straight, as a summons to the neighbouring nations, the Ammonites and the rest, to condole with Moab. Calvin denies that any pity is intended: it was not the prophet’s object to show that the Moabites deserved it, but by a figure to exaggerate how dreadful the judgment would be, so that all who had known that people should be smitten with terror, and the ruin be reckoned a prodigy by nations who thought them unassailable. On the broken staff the voices agree. Adam Clarke makes it the sceptre and the end of Moabite sovereignty, Wesley notes that a rod and a staff are ensigns of government as well as instruments for punishing offenders; Calvin makes the two words one thing and reads the question as spoken in the person of all nations, and Keil and Delitzsch render it the rod of strength and the staff of majesty.
18:
The sentence on Dibon turns on an irony the geographers supply. Adam Clarke places the city two leagues north of the Arnon and six east of the Dead Sea, anciently a city of the Reubenites and later held by Moab. Charles Ellicott adds that it stands in the Moabite Stone inscription as a royal city, fell to Reuben in the distribution and must later have been retaken, and under another form of the name is described as abounding in water. That detail gives the prophet his point: its waters will not save its people from the thirst that falls on those dragged into exile. John Wesley notices the same, that it was well watered and yet is threatened with thirst, and takes this to mean being driven into some dry country. John Calvin reads it more widely. Some, he says, make the word mean a dry land, which the verb dwell favours; but by thirst he understands the want of all things, set against glory, and worse than disgrace or poverty, since many pinched by want can still find a fountain, and to have no water at all is extreme misery.

At Aroer the question is which town. Ellicott finds two of the name, one north of the Arnon that passed from Sihon to Reuben to Moab, another in Ammonite territory near the Jabbok, and thinks both are meant where the older prophet speaks of the cities of Aroer; the name survives in a modern one, and he quotes Milton for the lie of the country. John Gill puts it on the Moabite border toward Ammon, near the Arnon. Clarke draws the practical inference, that a town at that distance must watch for its own safety and question every passenger, so as to know when to pack up and be gone. Calvin works instead on the grammar. The prophet shifts between one and many and between the genders, he says, to amplify: the crowd shows that the land will be emptied, the single man and woman that they will not go off in troops but be scattered as in a rout, one fleeing this way and another that, with no sex spared.

Calvin also explains why the passage is written as it is. The prophets did not describe calamity in so elevated a style out of care for fame, but because men were hard enough to despise a threatening or take it for a fable; so it had to be exaggerated by comparisons and, as he puts it, driven in with a hammer. The Jews would never have believed the Chaldeans could reach a people who lay like a hidden treasure, so the judgment is painted rather than described, to lead them to the scene itself.

Then the list of towns begins, and Calvin parts from the other commentators. Of these cities and their situation, he says, there is no need to say much, for it would be useless labour; the point is only that no part of the land is exempt. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott do the labour anyway. Both identify the places as towns of the table-land north of the Arnon that appear in the older books as belonging to Reuben, and both note that one is named nowhere else. Ellicott finds three of the names on the Moabite Stone, recalls that another was the scene of a famous battle between Sihon and the Israelites, and traces a fourth from Reuben to the Levites and so into Moabite hands; Keil and Delitzsch weigh where the ancient authorities placed that battlefield. On the cry to be raised, Clarke reads it as warning the country to provide for its own safety; Wesley notes that the name is properly a river, the district beside it probably taking its name from the water; and Gill makes the verse the answer the fugitives give to those who stopped them on the road.
22:
The roll of towns is mostly Charles Ellicott’s ground, and he reads the names for their meanings. Beth-diblathaim he renders the house of the double cake of figs, thinks it was applied to one of the more fertile districts, and identifies it with a station of the Israelites named between Dibon and the mountains of Abarim. Beth-gamul, the house of the camel, he cannot find in the earlier lists at all. Beth-meon he gives in its longer form as Beth-baal-meon, takes the second element for a citadel of heaven, and judges from its compounding with Baal that the place was a famous sanctuary of the Moabite god. John Gill stops at Kerioth for a different reason, noting that it once belonged to Judah and that some have derived the surname of Judas Iscariot from it, as though it meant a man of Kerioth.

Two of the names Ellicott cannot place without difficulty, and he sets the problem out honestly. Kerioth, plural in form and meaning simply cities, has been identified by one traveller with a ruined town near the Bozrah named beside it here; but both lie some sixty miles north of Heshbon, which has been thought fatal to the identification. Ellicott answers that the phrase far and near suggests the prophet is taking in the more distant cities to which Moabite power may have reached, and that another scholar proposes a site much closer, near Dibon and Beth-meon. He reports that Kerioth is called a place of palaces by an older prophet, and traces the second name, which means a fortification, through its appearance among the towns of Gilead and its later fame as the birthplace of a Roman emperor. Keil and Delitzsch place the whole list on the table-land north of the Arnon.

The horn and the arm are read the same way by everyone. Gill takes the horn for the kingdom itself, high and strong, by which Moab both defended himself and struck at others as a beast does. Adam Clarke says the political and physical powers alike are gone. John Wesley makes it the beauty and the strength of Moab. Ellicott notes that the horn of animals was the natural symbol of strength and passed easily to nations, and that the broken arm is one powerless to grasp sword or sceptre. John Calvin treats the second clause as the prophet’s own explanation of the first, and observes that God is brought forward as the speaker just here, because the Moabites believed the horn could not be broken and the prophet in his own name would not have been believed.

The command to make Moab drunk is addressed, Gill and Calvin agree, to the enemy: to the king of Babylon and his army, whom Calvin describes the prophet as summoning like a herald, remarking that the prophets showed how efficacious their doctrine was when they besieged cities and gave orders to armies. The cup is not wine, Gill says, but the vengeance of God, given him till he loses his senses and reels and staggers and falls; Wesley calls it the intoxicating wine of divine vengeance; Calvin explains the figure by saying that men overwhelmed with miseries are stunned out of reason and judgment as a drunkard is. Over the vomit they divide. Some, Calvin reports, understand it of intemperate joy and put the clause in the past tense, so that Moab shouted in his own vomit, luxuriating in his abundance; and he grants the contrast is not unsuitable, that one who exulted in prosperity should shortly become a derision. But he follows the generally approved reading, in which the vomit stands for excessive grief. Ellicott traces the image to the cup of divine fury in the earlier chapters and puts the shame plainly: as men looked with scorn on a drunkard wallowing, so they were to look on the nation that had been so boastful.
27:
The charge is that Moab laughed at a neighbour in ruin. John Gill dates it from the carrying away of the ten tribes by the Assyrians and then of Judah by the Chaldeans, and says the Moabites ought to have refrained on the common principles of humanity, the more so because they were kinsmen; by the law of retaliation it is just they be derided in their turn. Adam Clarke hears a taunt against the God of Israel as no better than other gods, and asks whether the Israelites had ever come to rob Moab, adding that this is what the Lord particularly resents. Charles Ellicott stops on the skipping for joy and calls it a gesture of triumphant malice, like the wagging of the head or the shrugging of the shoulders.

The question whether Israel was found among thieves divides the readings. Ellicott takes it as expecting the answer no, Israel not having been one of the lawless nations, and compares the question asked over the grave of Abner. But some critics, he reports, read the Hebrew particle as meaning when, which turns the clause into an admission that Israel had been an unjust invader, led into it by her alliances with the robber nations. John Calvin holds both halves at once. With regard to God the people deserved very severe scourges; but with regard to the Moabites they were innocent, for these could object nothing against them, being as bad or worse themselves. That doubles the crime, since they raged proudly and without cause. Behind it lies the principle that makes the offence religious: God has so adopted his Church that he counts wrong done to it as done to himself, and to touch them is to touch the apple of his eye.

The counsel to leave the cities for the rock is taken plainly. Gill says the strongest towns will be taken, so flight to the rocks is the only hope; Clarke sends them to the most inaccessible mountains; John Wesley notes that rocks are naturally fortified where walls are not; Ellicott observes that caves were always the asylum of fugitives there; and Keil and Delitzsch mark where the figure turns literal, adding that wild pigeons still nest in the clefts of high rocks in that country, over the yawning hollows. Calvin alone reads the imperative differently: it is not a command in the sense in which God commands what is right, but the prophet showing himself armed with the sword of God to perform as well as to speak; and the deserted places named mean not simple exile but removal to regions unknown and empty of men.

Who says we have heard the pride of Moab is disputed. Gill reports Kimchi holding it the prophet speaking in the name of the nations, but prefers the Lord himself, taking the plural for the plurality of persons in the Godhead and the singular that follows for the unity of the divine essence. Keil and Delitzsch answer a third way, that those who heard are the prophet and the people of God together; and they add that the accents point to quite another construction, followed by an old paraphrase, in which the doubtful word means staves and stands for princes who do not endure. Ellicott notices that the words are lifted from the older prophet, who seems to take a kind of pleasure in going back to them as showing the fault incurable; where the older passage left the whole speech to the people, this one inserts a clause of divine oracle. Calvin denies that hearing here means hearing by report: the Moabites were heralds of their own power, making a bellowing and seeking by their tongues to strike others with terror. He then sorts the words, the first meaning swelling and claiming more than belongs to one, the next rising high so as to look down on others.
30:
The thirtieth verse is the darkest in the chapter, and John Calvin says so: the second clause is variously explained, and he lists the renderings first. The word usually given as wrath he renders insolence, since it properly signifies excess, from a root meaning to pass over. The next word can mean branches of trees and sometimes sons, and some take it of sons here, as though no posterity would be left to continue the Moabite name; but that cannot stand, he says, since the chapter promises a residue, so the word must mean their empty boastings. The rectitude denied them, he adds, is not justice but stability: in his lies there is nothing that will hold. Charles Ellicott knows the same ambiguity, noting that the word can mean bars or staves as a symbol of defence, but keeps the received sense and finds the force of the verse in its repetition, the sentence of frustration falling on the wrath that breaks out in outrage and on the lies in which it looks for safety. John Gill and John Wesley keep it simple: God knows what Moab means to do, and it will never be done.

Who howls at the next verse is disputed four ways. Ellicott says the changes of person are remarkable and that the speaker is neither the Lord nor the prophet but an unnamed mourner, who appears in the third person in the next clause as representative of those who mourn; yet he allows that the prophet may be speaking out of sympathy. Keil and Delitzsch take that view outright, and note that where the older prophecy makes the mourning that of Moab before the prophet mingles his tears, this prophet, with his natural softness, begins the lament himself. Gill hears the prophet affected as a man with the miseries of a very wicked people, but thinks his design is to show what reason the Moabites had to howl, and reports Kimchi as making him speak in the person of that people. Calvin agrees, that the prophet is not telling us what he means to do but assuming the character of the sufferers, crying and muttering by turns, to set the calamity before the eye.

The stronghold named beside it divides them over its very name. Calvin reports that some take the last word as a proper name and render the whole the strong city, though by etymology it is the city of potsherd. Ellicott identifies it with the fortress called Kir of Moab, follows an old paraphrase to a modern town on a strong position in the mountains south-east of the Dead Sea, and takes the name to mean the City of the Sun, which may point to a connection with that kind of nature-worship.

At Sibmah the question is one small preposition. Gill gives three possibilities: weeping with the weeping of Jazer, or after it, taking up a new lament as the desolation moves on, or more than that weeping. Keil and Delitzsch set out the same three and prefer the first, confirmed by the older reading. Calvin argues from the older prophet the opposite way: since he wrote in rather than more than, the sense is a continued mourning to which there is no end, one city destroyed and then another giving fresh cause. He treats the vine as the whole wealth of the place, with the citizens for its shoots. On the ground Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree closely, both placing Jazer some fifteen miles north of Heshbon and Sibmah within a short walk of it, both noting that the vines must have been famous and that the region still yields excellent grapes. Ellicott traces Jazer from the Amorites through the Gadites into Moabite hands, and admits that the sea of Jazer must have been an inland lake nobody has identified. Wesley notes only that Jazer seems to have fallen first.
33:
The vintage shout is what the voices linger over. John Gill begins with the plentiful field, which stands for any fruitful place like Carmel, not the mountain in Israel, since the prophecy is of Moab. Charles Ellicott hears in the closing clause the song of the men who trod out the grapes, and finds the phrase like the Greek way of speaking of gifts that are no gifts, the shout that is no shout being turned to wailing, or replaced by the shout of battle. John Calvin works through the word at length. Some, he reports, render it by a Greek term for the call of sailors driving to shore and congratulating themselves on the harbour; but the word covers other work-songs, since reapers sing when they finish and the vine-dressers had songs of their own, sung, as Virgil records, by the worn-out vine-dresser at the last rows of the vines. The word stands twice in the verse, Calvin says, because men are excessive in their rejoicing at that season.

On the cry that runs across the country the geographers agree. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both put Heshbon and Elealeh about two miles apart, so that the panic-cry of one is echoed in the other, and Keil and Delitzsch add that both stood on hills, the second commanding the whole southern country, so a shout carried far. Calvin supposes the prophet chose cities lying opposite each other, so that the crying runs from one corner of the land to the other and no part of Moab is left quiet.

The heifer of three years old is read three ways. Ellicott reports that many critics take the words for a proper name and conjecture a town that was one of three of the same name, or a member of a triple city whose other members are the places just named; but nothing is known of such a town, and the epithet, meaning a heifer never brought under the yoke, would suit either place as a virgin fortress not yet taken. Calvin makes it a figure of wantonness: a heifer of that age frisks and leaps because it knows nothing of the yoke, and is neither worn by bearing nor drained by milking, so the comparison fits a people long unrestrained in their plenty. He then reports, fairly, a reason he calls more suitable than his own, that Moab in its distress is a heifer lowing for want of pasture and above all of water, which agrees with the drying of the waters in the next clause. Where those waters were, Ellicott cannot settle. Travellers had found a brook and ruins near the southern end of the Dead Sea; the place of the same name in the older books lies too far north; another identified it with a valley near the fords of the Jordan. Calvin notes only that the older prophet calls them the brooks of the willows, and concludes they flowed perpetually.

The last verse of the passage stops the worship. Gill takes the man who offers in the high places for the priest, and says all will be carried away, so that none is left to sacrifice. Ellicott infers that pilgrimages to the sanctuary of Chemosh on the Moabite mountains were a prominent feature of the national life, and that the conquest would end them. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to make the disputed word a noun, since that would destroy the parallelism, and refuse the rendering one who raises a high place, the verb not bearing that sense. Calvin makes the point that God avenges the idolatry with the pride and cruelty. The Moabites came of a pious father, being the posterity of Lot, and had renounced the true God; and if he did not spare them, who never received the law, Calvin asks how those shall escape in whose ears the Word of God sounds daily.
36:
Whose heart sounds like pipes is the question of the earlier lament over again. Charles Ellicott takes the prophet at his word: his heart becomes as it were musical in its groans, and he cannot look on the panic-stricken city without sharing its misery. John Gill reports Kimchi to the contrary, that he speaks in the person of the Moabites, whose hearts would sound like the doleful noise of minstrels. John Calvin agrees, holding that the prophet transfers to himself the feelings of others so that the event may be set before the eyes, since the wealth of Moab then dazzled everybody and the vengeance was hard to imagine. On the instrument they agree that it is a funeral one. John Wesley says such pipes as were used at funerals; Ellicott adds that the pipe is chosen rather than the harp because it had become the recognised music for burials; and Calvin declines to settle whether the word means mourning pipes or bagpipes, remarking only that what is too refined he leaves alone. On the riches that perish, Calvin says the versions differ widely and prefers reserves, what had been laid up and thought safe; Keil and Delitzsch render it savings.

The signs of mourning are listed by everyone and moralised by one. Gill describes the plucking of the hair and the shaving of the beard, which he says Kimchi calls the glory of a face; Adam Clarke marks them as signs of the deepest distress; Ellicott calls them the wonted signs of mourning for the dead; Keil and Delitzsch note that the cuts are scratches inflicted on the body. Calvin alone objects to them. Sackcloth and ashes he allows as almost innate in human nature, but pulling off the beard and tearing the hands and face with the nails he calls excesses agreeable neither to men nor women, unfitting the one on the ground of modesty and the other of manliness. Mankind never keep a measure, he says, and are carried to excess whether they mourn or rejoice. Worse, the symbols God appointed to lead men to humble themselves were diverted to another end, that the mourner might look wretched to his neighbours and make a display of his tears; so hypocrisy was added to excess. Then he stops himself: there is no reason to dispute about mourning here, the prophet meaning only that they would be most miserable.

Why the lamentation is on the housetops they explain differently. Ellicott says the flat roof of an eastern house was the natural gathering place in a panic, as in peacetime for prayer or meditation or festive meetings. Calvin makes it deliberate, that they climb up to be more seen and to excite pity, and howl there.

The broken vessel closes the passage. Ellicott recalls that the prophet had made the image familiar by breaking a vessel himself as a sign. Calvin corrects the versions, which all render it a useless vessel where the Hebrew has a vessel with no delight in it, and draws the distinction he thinks it was made for: God chastises his own children when they sin, but never ceases to love them or hold them precious, whereas Moab is despised and thrown away. At the howling Gill notes that the first word may mean broken or thrown into consternation, and that Jarchi took it for an imperative; Ellicott prefers the Hebrew order, how is she broken down, how do they howl, and observes that the parallel with the older prophecy ends here. Calvin notes that the past tense stands for the future, that the closing word is better read terror than bruising, and that the astonishment is written in for the Jews, so that when the ruin came and men cried out that it was past understanding, they might know the prophecy had been in earnest.
40:
The eagle is agreed on, then disputed. John Gill makes it Nebuchadnezzar with his army, compared to that bird for strength, swiftness and greed after prey, and John Wesley agrees; Charles Ellicott calls it the natural symbol of a fierce invader and notices that it gains fresh vividness from the earlier picture of Moab as a dove nesting in the clefts of the rock, adding that the same verse is used again of Edom. John Calvin takes the wings the other way from what a reader might expect. The spreading is not to cherish, as an eagle spreads over its young, but by extension: the Chaldeans would seize the whole land, so that no corner would be missed.

Whether Kerioth is a city or a common noun they split over. Gill reports that Jarchi and others take it for a town, while Kimchi and Abarbinel make it an appellative and render it the cities, every one taken as easily as a single city, the cities of the plain answering to the strongholds on the heights. Ellicott notes that the word carries the article and would render it the cities, painting the wide devastation coming on all the fortresses; and Calvin translates it that way outright. On the failing courage Calvin is full. The Moabites boasted of military valour though they had made no recent trial of it, despising their enemies on the credit of old deeds; the prophet answers that their hearts will be softer than a woman in her worst distress. Behind that he sets a doctrine: it is in the power of God to melt the hearts of men, so that lions become does, and courage is not only a gift but one that must be renewed daily in those who have it. Ellicott observes that the phrase occurs in only one other place.

Over the destruction from being a people, Gill and Adam Clarke stand furthest apart. Gill holds it means for a time and not for ever, since the chapter closes by promising the captivity of Moab shall be returned, or else that they should cease to be the people they had been; he reports Abarbinel taking it comparatively, that Moab should be destroyed more than any other people, but prefers his own. Clarke reads it hard: they shall have neither king nor governor, and he doubts there is evidence they were ever reinstated in their national character. Many probably returned with the Jews on the edict of Cyrus, he grants, but as to their being an independent nation afterwards he asks where the proof is. Calvin is interested in the reason rather than the extent, and repeats that the Moabites never claimed to be equal with God; it was in raising their crests against his people that they became contumelious against him, since he had promised to protect them. From this he draws a warning against wronging the godly and a comfort, that whoever molests us is making war on God.

The three words of the closing threat are read as one hunt. Ellicott says the sequence shows each word playing its own part, first the terror of the animal driven by huntsmen, then the pit dug for it, then the trap that secures it if it scrambles out; and the phrase, he notes, had probably passed into proverbial use. Gill takes it as a proverb meaning that escape from one judgment lands a man in a greater. Calvin marks the alliteration of the three words and paraphrases it as one motion, fear driving them out, the pit waiting in the road, the snare closing on whoever climbs out. On the year of visitation he turns pastoral: the clause keeps the godly from fainting under long delay, since we would have God always act in haste and rebel when he calls us to patience, not considering that the fitness of times is his to determine.
45:
Two words at the head of the passage are read four ways. John Gill lays them out: the fugitives stood under the shadow of Heshbon because of the strength of that city, as Kimchi held; or for fear of their enemies, as his father held; or for want of strength, having none left to flee with, as Jarchi and Abarbinel held. Gill himself would turn the sentence round, so that those standing under the shadow of Heshbon now flee with all the strength they have. Charles Ellicott renders it simply without strength: the fugitives seek shelter there and find none. John Calvin notes that the word for strength stands alone in the Hebrew and that some attach it to the verb stood, which he thinks preferable.

That the fire out of Heshbon is a quotation everyone agrees. Adam Clarke says the prophet borrowed it from an ancient poet whom Moses quotes, and Ellicott identifies the fragment as probably from the old book of the wars of the Lord. On what the fire is, Calvin parts from the majority. Most, he says, make it the spoiler who was to come; but he thinks the two cities are themselves the beginnings of the fire, since there the counsels were taken which provoked the Chaldeans. Wars are not contrived in villages, he observes; the great cities gather the wood and kindle the flame. Ellicott keeps to the picture: the Moabites come under the walls for shelter and the fire bursts out of walls and gates, while the tumultuous ones are literally children of tumult, the clamorous panic-stricken crowds. Clarke takes that last phrase to mean the choicest persons of the whole nation.

The cry of woe is brief in every mouth but one. Gill observes that they are called the people of Chemosh as Israel were called the people of the Lord, and that the idol they trusted could not keep them; Clarke notes only that he was their supreme god. Calvin makes something of the exclamation itself: the prophet cries out as though words failed him, and there is more force in the one word than in any long description. He marks the softening too, since ruin was threatened before and now only exile is named; but captivity, he answers, is a kind of death, for it abolishes the name of a nation.

The last verse turns, and the voices divide over how far. Gill allows a literal accomplishment under Cyrus, observes from Josephus that they were still a people when Alexander and a later king subdued them, and adds a spiritual fulfilment in the conversion of some under the Gospel, Kimchi referring the words to the days of the Messiah; the present inhabitants of that country, he thinks, will be converted when the fulness of the Gentiles is brought in. Clarke will not have the literal half. The expressions of total destruction are too strong and frequent to leave room for a limited interpretation; many returned on the edict of Cyrus, but neither the Moabites nor the Ammonites nor even the Jews were ever restored to their national consequence, and the conversion of the remnant to the Gospel must be the main end designed. John Wesley agrees in a line, calling it a spiritual return into the kingdom of the Messiah. Calvin holds together what looks contradictory, ruin near and yet a remnant to renew the name of the nation, and says the promise was given not for Moab but that the Jews might be assured of pardon, God stretching out his hand to aliens as it were accidentally so that his own people might taste his favour; and from that nation, he adds, the Redeemer of the world drew his descent. Ellicott notices how characteristic this far-off hope is of these later chapters, and suspects the closing formula is an editorial note marking the end of a section.
